screens.title: Installing and Running Prometheus
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this session we'll make Prometheus come alive on a Linux machine. screens.title: Prometheus binary and bundled files
screens.narratorSegment: Prometheus is distributed as a small archive that contains a few key elements: the Prometheus server binary, a utility called promtool, and a default configuration file named prometheus. yml. The server binary is the runtime that scrapes targets, stores time series data, and responds to queries. Promtool is a helper you can run to validate and check your configuration files before launching the server; it reduces wasted time caused by YAML syntax errors. The default prometheus. yml gives you a minimal starting point with a global section and example scrape configs. For example, the bundled configuration often already contains a self-scrape job so you can boot the server and immediately verify that prometheus_up is reporting one. A common misconception is that Prometheus has many runtime dependencies; in practice, the binary is self-contained which makes it robust and simple to install. As a concrete example, after extracting the archive you will see a prometheus executable, promtool, and a prometheus. yml. Inspecting these files is a quick way to understand an installation before changing anything. Takeaway: know your files, validate configuration with promtool, and use the default prometheus. yml as a safe template to start scraping.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Prometheus binary and bundled files
Definition & purpose

The archive includes three practical components: the Prometheus server binary, promtool for configuration validation, and a default prometheus.yml that shows a minimal working setup. Understanding each file prevents mistakes when you customize your deployment.

Server binary
Runs scrapes, stores series, and serves the web UI and query API.
promtool
Validates the prometheus.yml so you catch YAML errors before runtime.
prometheus.yml
Defines global intervals, scrape_configs, and initial example jobs you can adapt.
Concrete example
What you see after extraction
A directory containing the prometheus executable, promtool, console libraries, and a prometheus.yml. Inspecting these files helps you decide where to place them on the system and how to run the server.
Common mistake
Editing the prometheus.yml before understanding its structure can introduce indentation errors. Always validate with promtool before launching Prometheus.
Key Takeaway
Know what is in the archive, validate configs with promtool, and use the default file as a safe starting point.

screens.title: Structure of prometheus.yml
screens.narratorSegment: The prometheus. yml file is the central configuration for a Prometheus server. It contains a global section where default parameters like the scrape interval and evaluation interval are set, and a scrape_configs section where you define jobs that tell Prometheus which HTTP endpoints to scrape. Each job has a job_name, and inside a job you usually configure static_configs listing target endpoints. For example, a job named prometheus can include a static target of localhost on the default metrics port so Prometheus scrapes itself. Knowing this structure is essential because it determines which metrics are collected and how often. A typical misconception is thinking every target must be a separate job; in fact, one job may include multiple static targets grouped logically. As a concrete example, set global scrape_interval to 15 seconds to control how frequently the server pulls metrics. When you modify these values, remember they affect storage and query resolution: more frequent scrapes increase data retention and resource use. Key takeaway: edit global settings only after considering scrape frequency and define jobs with clear job_name and static_configs so your targets are discovered consistently.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Structure of prometheus.yml
Core sections explained
  • global: default scrape_interval and evaluation_interval that apply to all jobs unless overridden.
  • scrape_configs: a list of jobs that tell Prometheus which endpoints to scrape.
  • job_name: a label applied to metrics from that job to identify origin.
  • static_configs: explicit target addresses such as localhost:9090 for each job.
Misconception check: you do not need a separate job per endpoint; group related targets in one job unless different scrape settings are required.
Visual quick-reference
global:
- scrape_interval: 15s - evaluation_interval: 15s
scrape_configs:
- job_name: 'prometheus' static_configs: - targets: ['localhost:9090']
Key Takeaway
Understand global defaults and structure scrape_configs logically so your jobs and targets reflect how you want metrics grouped and collected.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Minimal prometheus.yml
YAML example to copy
global:
  scrape_interval: 15s
  evaluation_interval: 15s

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'prometheus'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['localhost:9090']
Notes: metrics_path and scheme default to /metrics and http. This minimal file is intentionally small so you can quickly verify the server, then extend scrape_configs when you add more targets.
Validation & common pitfalls
Before running
  • Ensure you use spaces, not tabs, and consistent indentation levels.
  • Run the configuration utility to validate the file for syntax errors.
  • If you change ports, update the target address accordingly.
Key Takeaway
A small, validated prometheus.yml that scrapes localhost allows you to prove the server is running before adding complexity.

screens.title: Running Prometheus and reading logs
screens.narratorSegment: Starting Prometheus is a straightforward step but watching the logs helps you confirm the server health. You will launch the server while specifying which configuration file to use. On startup Prometheus logs a sequence of messages: it announces that the server is ready to receive web requests, starts the target manager, and prints information about loaded configuration. These log messages are your primary clues: if Prometheus finds malformed YAML it will log parse errors and exit; if port binding fails it will show an address in use message. A common learner mistake is to assume a silent prompt indicates success; instead, read the logs to confirm the server state. As a concrete example, after starting Prometheus you should see the lines indicating the server is ready and the target manager is starting. If errors appear, use promtool to test your config and resolve any syntactic issues. Takeaway: start Prometheus with the intended config and use the startup logs as the first source of truth for diagnosing failures or confirming success. Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Running Prometheus and reading logs
Startup checklist
Provide the path to your prometheus.yml when starting the server so it loads the intended configuration and you can read the resulting log messages.
Key log indicators
  • Server ready to receive web requests – indicates the web UI should be available.
  • Starting target manager – indicates scrape jobs are being scheduled.
  • Configuration parse errors – indicates prometheus.yml issues requiring fix.
  • Address already in use – indicates a port conflict you must resolve.
Example log snippets
Server ready to receive web requests Starting target manager Loaded configuration file
Troubleshoot
If you see address binding errors, change the listening port or stop the process using that port. If YAML parse errors appear, validate with promtool and correct indentation.
Key Takeaway
Use logs as the primary diagnostic source. They tell you whether the server bound correctly and whether your config parsed successfully.

screens.title: Verify Prometheus using the Web UI
screens.narratorSegment: Verifying that Prometheus is working involves the built-in web user interface. After the server starts, open a browser to the server's web UI on the configured port and navigate to the status page for targets. The targets view lists each job and target, its last scrape time, and its status, which should be UP for healthy endpoints. For Prometheus itself, look for a job named prometheus with target localhost on the server's port. To confirm in metric form, run a simple query for prometheus_up which returns a value of one for targets that Prometheus is scraping successfully. A common misunderstanding is assuming a running process always implies successful scraping; the web UI provides a clear, immediate view of which targets are being scraped and the result of the latest attempt. As an example, if prometheus_up returns zero for the prometheus job, it indicates Prometheus cannot reach that endpoint. The practical takeaway is to use the targets page and a prometheus_up query together to verify both server availability and scraping success. screens.title: Using promtool and manual checks
screens.narratorSegment: There are three complementary checks you should use when validating a Prometheus startup: configuration validation with promtool, reading startup logs, and inspecting the web UI. promtool is designed to catch syntax and indentation issues in prometheus. yml before you attempt to start the server, saving you from parse failures. Reading logs shows you runtime information such as whether the server bound to the requested address and whether the target manager started. The web UI provides a live confirmation that targets are being scraped and that prometheus_up indicates success. A common mistake is relying on only one of these checks; for instance, promtool may say the config is valid but the server could still fail to bind to a port already in use. Conversely, seeing an UP state in the UI does not replace careful review of logs when intermittent scraping failures appear. As an example workflow: run promtool first to validate syntax, start Prometheus and watch logs, then finish by confirming targets are UP in the UI. The combined approach minimizes surprises and gives you a clear path to diagnose where a failure lives.

screens.title: Port conflicts, web listen address, and firewall issues
screens.narratorSegment: Connection refused or an address already in use error are among the most frequent startup problems. These errors mean Prometheus attempted to bind its web interface to a port that is unavailable. To diagnose, first review the startup logs to find the exact binding error. If another process is using the default port, you can either stop that process or run Prometheus on a different port by changing the listening address configuration or flag. Another frequent cause of inaccessible web UI is a firewall blocking the port; confirm firewall rules allow traffic to the Prometheus port. A common misconception is thinking a failed browser connection always means Prometheus did not start; in some cases Prometheus is running but the port is blocked. As a practical example: if the web UI cannot be reached but logs show the server is ready, check firewall settings and the listening address. Takeaway: use logs to find binding errors, then either free the port, change the listening address, or adjust firewall rules to restore access. Typical causes
  • Another service already bound to the same port.
  • Firewall rules blocking the port.
  • Server bound to localhost only while you try a remote connection.
Quick fixes
Free the port by stopping the conflicting process or use an alternate port.
Adjust firewall rules to allow inbound access to the Prometheus port.
Change the web listening address to bind to a different port if needed.
Diagnostic flow
  1. Read the Prometheus logs for an address binding error.
  2. Identify the process using the port or select an alternate port.
  3. Adjust firewall rules if the server is running but unreachable remotely.

Treat binding errors as configuration or environment issues, not Prometheus failures. Logs indicate the corrective action to take.

screens.title: Common assessment and troubleshooting questions
screens.narratorSegment: When assessing a student's install, two compact diagnostic questions are very instructive. First, if accessing the web UI returns a connection refused error, the most likely causes are that the Prometheus server failed to start or that it's bound to a port different from the one you tried. The correct troubleshooting approach is to check the terminal where Prometheus was launched for error messages, look for binding or configuration parse errors, confirm promtool validation, and, if the logs show the server started successfully, inspect network and firewall rules. Second, questions about the scrape_interval and evaluation_interval are useful to check conceptual understanding: scrape_interval controls how often Prometheus pulls metrics from targets, while evaluation_interval controls how often rules and alerting evaluations run. A misconception is to expect these values to be independent of storage implications; in reality, shorter scrape intervals create more time series data and higher resource use. In a short assessment, ask the learner to explain each parameter's role, give an example with fifteen second intervals, and describe how to proceed when the web UI is unreachable. The learner should demonstrate log inspection, config validation, and a reasoned next step to restore access.

Welcome. In this session we'll make Prometheus come alive on a Linux machine. You'll learn the practical steps: download a precompiled Prometheus archive, extract it, inspect the bundled files, and run the server with a simple configuration that scrapes Prometheus itself. We'll also cover how the essential prometheus. yml sections work, how to validate that file, and how to check the web UI to confirm that the target is UP. This matters because a working Prometheus instance is the foundation for any monitoring setup: if the server can't start or scrape itself, downstream metrics, alerts, and dashboards won't be reliable. As a concrete example, you'll see a minimal prometheus. yml that sets a global scrape interval and a single scrape job called prometheus which targets localhost on the default port. A common misconception is that Prometheus needs complex dependencies; in fact, it runs as a standalone binary and is intentionally simple to install. By the end of the lesson you'll be able to run Prometheus, validate the configuration, and confirm the prometheus_up metric. Consider this your practical checklist for a first successful install.

Third, you will run the Prometheus server, check its logs for startup messages, and confirm the prometheus_up metric using the web user interface. Prometheus is distributed as a small archive that contains a few key elements: the Prometheus server binary, a utility called promtool, and a default configuration file named prometheus. yml. When assessing a student's install, two compact diagnostic questions are very instructive. First, if accessing the web UI returns a connection refused error, the most likely causes are that the Prometheus server failed to start or that it's bound to a port different from the one you tried. Second, questions about the scrape_interval and evaluation_interval are useful to check conceptual understanding: scrape_interval controls how often Prometheus pulls metrics from targets, while evaluation_interval controls how often rules and alerting evaluations run. A misconception is to expect these values to be independent of storage implications; in reality, shorter scrape intervals create more time series data and higher resource use.
